name: Potter's wheel in Mesopotamia
summary: Potters in Mesopotamia began shaping coil-built bowls on a rotating wheel around 3900 to 3800 BCE, the start of wheel-made pottery there.
description: Potters in northern Mesopotamia and in the Uruk communities of the south adopted the potter's wheel in the early 4th millennium BCE, around 3900 to 3800 BCE. They used it for wheel-coiling: a vessel was built from coils of clay and then shaped on the turning wheel. Throughout the 4th millennium vessels were wheel-coiled and not thrown from a lump of clay; the first were few and small, mostly bowls made by a handful of specialists. Wheel-coiled pottery is reported earlier, in the mid-5th millennium BCE, in the Levant.

impact.note: Scored on the general view, not on the cited pages: wheel-made pottery became the workshop norm across Western Asia and its neighbours, but with an earlier Levantine wheel and possibly separate wheels in East Asia this record's own share is held at reach 2; it made an existing craft faster and more regular (depth 1) and a long line of wheel-shaping and later wheel-throwing followed (generativity 2).

date.label: around 3900–3800 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Archaeological evidence indicates that wheel-coiling was adopted in northern Mesopotamia in the early 4th millennium BCE, around 3900 to 3800 BCE.

evidence.supports: chronological coincidence with northern Mesopotamia – supported by archaeological evidence (Baldi, 2013; Vallet et al., 2017) indicating an adoption of wheel-coiling in the early 4th millennium (around 3900–3800 BCE)

evidence.locator: Tell Feres case study and Figs. 2–4
evidence.supports: Excavated northern Mesopotamian bowls in later LC2 strata show microstructural coil joints and rotation marks.

date.label: 4th millennium BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Throughout the 4th millennium BCE, north-Mesopotamian and Uruk vessels made on the wheel were wheel-coiled, not thrown.

evidence.supports: 4th millennium north-Mesopotamian and Uruk vessels were always wheel-coiled (rather than thrown), the use of these turntables capable of developing a limited speed and RKE is entirely plausible.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Write a separate record for wheel-coiling in the mid-5th millennium BCE southern Levant (Baldi and Roux 2016; Roux and de Miroschedji 2009), which is earlier than Mesopotamia and is the likelier first known use of the potter's wheel.
Establish when and where vessels were first truly thrown on a fast wheel; Baldi notes stone potter's wheel components only from the 3rd millennium BCE onwards.
Check the Dawenkou and Longshan fast wheel in China for independence; it may need its own record.
Establish the Cucuteni-Trypillia wheel claim and the Ur wheelhead date from excavation reports.

research.note: Baldi (2021) reports wheel-coiled pottery in the mid-5th millennium Levant, earlier than in Mesopotamia, and leaves open whether Mesopotamian potters borrowed the technique or developed it from rotary devices already in local use.

links.statement: Did the use of pivoted pottery supports in the Late Ubaid workshop contribute to the later introduction of wheel-coiling at Tell Feres?
links.caveats: The reports describe a possible early rotary support and diagnostic wheel-coiled bowls at the same site, several centuries apart. The excavators cannot trace use through the intervening stages or identify an inherited tool design.

evidence.locator: Tell Feres case study and Fig. 2
evidence.supports: Distinguishes a possible early pivot-mounted disc from later shaping by rotary kinetic energy.
Raises Ubaid rotary devices as a predecessor to investigate. The article does not demonstrate continuity from a particular device.
